analysis.title: What does the US-Iran conflict mean for markets?
key_insights: Brent crude has fallen for three consecutive weeks, taking its November month-to-date decline to 21.5%, on course for the first monthly decline in five months.
Petro-Logistics estimates Gulf crude and condensate exports reached about 19.5 mbpd in October, close to the pre-war 19.9 mbpd seen in February. US naval escorts helped the recovery.

The physical oil market has not normalized. There were 19 reported and confirmed attacks on ships in the first 18 days of November, and Middle East refined-product exports remain well below pre-war levels.
US military support carries substantial costs, and it is unclear how long the US will sustain this level of involvement.

China is stepping up crude imports and global inventory buffers remain depleted. The IEA estimates observed inventories are down 462 million barrels since the war began, with on-land stocks at their lowest since at least 2016.
UBS sees an attractive near-term risk-reward in crude and expects prices to recover.
Positioning is cleaner after the sell-off. Money managers cut Brent net longs to the lowest in over four months, and WTI net longs are at the lowest since January.
UBS favors diversified commodity exposure across energy, precious metals, industrial metals and agriculture as protection against prolonged supply disruption and inflation pressure.
New events: US forces struck a missile launch site on Iran's Qeshm Island on 20 November, and Iran's navy claimed two oil tankers hit mines east of the Strait of Hormuz, with one catching fire.

sector_views.rationale: Broad commodity exposure diversifies portfolios and hedges prolonged energy disruption and inflation risk.
Crude is seen as attractive near term after a 21.5% November decline, with inventories depleted and shipping attacks continuing.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Sharp sell-off on recovering Gulf exports, which UBS views as an overshoot given the unnormalized physical market.
Export volumes nearly recovered, but refined products and inventories lag.
Rising Chinese buying adds demand support and draws on depleted inventories.

trade_ideas.description: Long crude oil, plus broad diversified commodity exposure across energy, precious metals, industrial metals and agriculture
trade_ideas.rationale: Attractive near-term risk-reward after the sell-off, with depleted inventories and fragile energy flows.
trade_ideas.risk: US withdrawal of naval escorts or renewed attacks would disrupt supply, while a lasting normalization of Gulf flows would pressure prices.

risk_factors: The US may not sustain naval escorts given the costs.
Renewed ship attacks and mining could cause prolonged supply disruption.
Further Gulf export normalization could push oil lower.
vol_and_positioning: Money managers cut Brent net-long positions to the lowest in more than four months.
WTI net longs are at the lowest level since January, so positioning looks considerably cleaner.
geopolitical: US forces struck a missile launch site on Iran's Qeshm Island on 20 November.
Iran's navy claimed two oil tankers hit mines east of the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, with one catching fire.
US naval escorts support Gulf crude flows, but how long the US will sustain involvement is unclear.
19 confirmed attacks on ships in the first 18 days of November.

tension_points.bull_case: Inventories are depleted by 462 million barrels, ship attacks continue, refined exports are weak and China is buying more, so prices should recover.
tension_points.bear_case: Gulf crude exports have nearly returned to the pre-war level of 19.9 mbpd with US naval escorts, which drove the 21.5% fall.
tension_points.what_invalidates: US escorts being withdrawn would worsen the bull case's supply risk, while a full normalization of Gulf exports including refined products would undermine it.

theme_stances.key_argument: The rebound in Gulf exports should not be mistaken for a normalization of the oil market, so crude should recover.
theme_stances.evidence: should not be mistaken for a normalization of the oil market
